chapter_theme: Self-restraint is the treasure that decides one's end. It works through body, speech and mind, and the chapter is most vivid on the tongue, whose burn alone never heals.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: restraint's excellence in general (121-125), restraint of body (126), of speech (127-129), and of mind (130).

121.reading: Restraint leads one among the immortals, and lack of restraint drives one into thick darkness.
121.nuance: Both verbs are of driving, so restraint is itself a force that carries a person. The final உய்த்துவிடும் has a sense of finality.

positions.position: The destinations are literal: the gods' world and a particular hell called darkness.
The results are this-worldly: lasting renown and a darkened life.
positions.quote: அடக்கம் அழியாத புகழைக் கொடுக்கும். அடங்காமை வாழ்வையே இருளாக்கி விடும்.

122.reading: Guard restraint as your wealth, for life has no greater gain than it.
122.nuance: Restraint is pictured as something to guard, as misers guard money, so the language of acquisition is turned to its opposite. Parimelazhagar notes this concerns humans, who can understand it and benefit.

123.reading: If one understands and keeps restrained in the right way, the restraint, recognised, will yield distinction.
123.nuance: The syntax is knotted, and the commentators parse the repeated அறிந்து differently: Parimelazhagar says one learns that restraint is itself knowledge, and Manakkudavar says one learns the five objects and the five organs. I'm unsure which is closest.

124.reading: The stature of one who is restrained and doesn't stray from his station is much greater than a mountain's.
124.nuance: தோற்றம், how one looks or appears, makes this a visual comparison. The dispute over நிலை decides whether the verse has a social hierarchy in it.

positions.position: The station is household life, and the restraint is exercised while enjoying sense objects.
The station is the order of varna and stage of life.
It's a matter of firmness of mind joined to unostentatious restraint.
positions.quote: உறுதியான உள்ளமும், அத்துடன் ஆர்ப்பாட்டமற்ற அடக்க உணர்வும்

125.reading: Bowing is good for all, and among them, for the rich it is a further wealth.
125.nuance: Parimelazhagar asks why the rich are singled out. Those with learning or birth may be humble without it being notable, but for the rich it stands out. Manakkudavar reads செல்வம் simply as abundance, which weakens the pun.

126.reading: If in one birth one can draw in the five like a tortoise, it is a protection for seven births.
126.nuance: The tortoise withdraws out of self-protection, and the image suggests retreat from danger, not conquest. The numbers one and seven make for an argument about return on effort. Kalaignar translates the seven births as all time.

127.reading: Whatever else they fail to guard, let them guard the tongue; if they don't, they'll suffer from the fault of their words.
127.nuance: This is a rare concession in a demanding chapter: it sets priorities for someone who cannot do everything. The opening யாகாவாராயினும் accepts failure in advance.

128.reading: If even one bad word has its effect, it turns out that nothing is good.
128.nuance: The verse doesn't say what stops being good, and the commentators offer three scopes, from one's speech to one's whole moral record.

positions.position: One harm caused by evil words turns the good of the speaker's other virtues to evil.
positions.quote: அவனுக்குப் பிற அறங்களான் உண்டான நன்மை தீதாய்விடும்.

positions.position: It concerns a word sweet to the hearer but harmful in effect, so flattery is also bad.
One bad word in a speech spoils all of that speech's good words, like poison in milk.

129.reading: A wound burned by fire heals inside, but a scar burned by the tongue doesn't heal.
129.nuance: புண் and வடு are carefully chosen: Parimelazhagar notes the first heals and is a wound, while the second stays and is a scar. For him the fire's mark may stay on the body but is healed in the mind, which reverses what one expects to be permanent.

130.reading: Virtue itself looks for its moment and enters by the path to the one who has guarded against anger and has learned restraint.
130.nuance: The usual relation is reversed: virtue is a seeker waiting on a person. Parimelazhagar's gloss of செவ்வி pictures virtue as a petitioner awaiting a good moment to present its plea. Manakkudavar adds what must be restrained: the pride that comes from learning.

links.note: The five senses are imagined as animals in both cases. In 24 they're elephants controlled by a goad, and in 126 they're a tortoise's limbs drawn in. One is control by force and the other is retreat to safety.

The renouncer quenches the five in 25. In 124, on Parimelazhagar's reading, the householder is restrained while enjoying the senses and is also called greater than a mountain. They are two different pictures of what restraint is.

Both say that no gain surpasses this, in the same formula (ஊங்கு), but 32 says it of virtue and 122 of restraint. The superlatives compete, as also in 61 on children, which suggests that the formula praises and doesn't actually rank.

In both அறம் acts like a person, and Parimelazhagar calls it a deity in both. In 77 it burns the loveless like the sun, and here it waits for the restrained like a petitioner. It's the same power with opposite manners.

Harsh speech in 100 is merely a stupid choice of raw fruit. In 129 it leaves a scar that never heals. The first chapter on speech treats the speaker's loss, and this one treats the listener's lasting injury.

In 109 one good act erases even murderous harm. In 128 one bad word turns all good to nothing. The ledgers are asymmetric, though the verses keep different books: the first is the recipient's memory, and the second, in Parimelazhagar's reading, is the speaker's merit.

source_issues: Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 130 has apparent slips: செல்வி for செவ்வி and நெற்றியின்கண் for நெறியின்கண்.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 122 and 126.
